problem: A particle $P$ of mass $4\,kg$ moves along the $x$-axis under the action of a resultant force. The particle's acceleration is $(4t+1)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $t\ge 0$ is the time in seconds. If the particle has velocity $v=3\,m/s$ when $t=0\,s,$ calculate the work done by the force between the times $t=1\,s$ and $t=2\,s.$
worked_solution:
The work-energy principle states that the work done by a resultant force on a particle equals the change in the particle's kinetic energy. That is,

$$
W=Δ\,\text{KE}
$$

where the change in kinetic energy of a particle is given by

$$
Δ\,\text{KE}=\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{1}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}m{v}_{0}^{2}
$$

and $m$ is the particle's mass, ${v}_{0}$ is its initial velocity, and ${v}_{1}$ is its final velocity.

The acceleration of the particle is given by $a(t)=4t+1,$ where $t$ is time in seconds.
We find the velocity $v(t)$ of the particle by integrating the acceleration with respect to time:

$$
\begin{aligned}v(t) & =\int a(t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =\int (4t+1)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2{t}^{2}+t+C\end{aligned}
$$

To determine $C,$ we use the fact that $v(0)=3.$ Substituting this into the above gives

$$
3=2(0)^{2}+0+C\,⟹\,C=3.
$$

Therefore, the velocity of the particle at time $t$ is $v(t)=2{t}^{2}+t+3.$
In particular, the particle's initial velocity, at $t=1$, is

$$
{v}_{0}=v(1)=2(1)^{2}+1+3=6\,m/s,
$$

and final velocity, at $t=2$, is

$$
{v}_{1}=v(2)=2(2)^{2}+2+3=13\,m/s.
$$

Therefore, by the work-energy principle, the work done by the force between these times is

$$
\begin{aligned}W & =Δ\,\text{KE} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {13}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\cdot 4\cdot {6}^{2} \\  & =338-72 \\  & =266\,J.\end{aligned}
$$
